title: EAM Maintenance Software: What It Is and How to Choose It
summary: EAM maintenance software connects daily maintenance with asset lifecycle decisions. Learn what to evaluate, how free models differ, and where AI fits.
body_markdown:
## **Key Takeaways**


-


EAM maintenance software ensures each asset’s repair history is usable for finance, operations, and other sites long after the work order closes.


-


The more teams and sites that work from the same asset history, the stronger the case for EAM over a focused CMMS.


-


Most of the work in an EAM rollout happens outside the software, in cleaning up and organizing asset data.


-


AI and predictive features in EAM are only as useful as the condition data and workflow behind them.


In many maintenance teams, a closed work order is the end of the trail. The repair is logged, but nobody uses that record when deciding whether to replace the asset or how much to budget for it next year. EAM maintenance software connects that history to those decisions. The question is whether your operation needs those connections enough to justify the extra cleanup, integration, and setup work involved with this solution.


## **What Is EAM Maintenance Software?**


EAM maintenance software is a maintenance platform that runs and records day-to-day work, such as work orders, inspections, and preventive maintenance (PM) and keeps that history attached to each asset for its whole life. That equips other teams with the same record: Finance can plan replacements, operations can compare sites, and the ERP can track parts and repair costs using one unified log.


[EAM software](https://upkeep.com/enterprise-asset-management-eam/) comes with a variety of different features, so the right choice depends on what assets you have and their regulations.


## **EAM Maintenance Software vs. CMMS**


Features alone make a poor dividing line between[these two software types](https://upkeep.com/learning/eam-or-cmms-systems/) , because a modern[computerized maintenance management system (CMMS)](https://upkeep.com/blog/what-is-cmms/) can already handle multiple sites, mobile work, integrations, analytics, and even AI features. EAM software covers the same work and carries each asset’s record further into capital plans and the company’s financial systems. Scope provides a better delineation: what the maintenance record has to support after the work is done.


If the system mainly needs to plan, assign, complete, and document maintenance work, a CMMS may be enough. If finance needs the same asset records for replacement budgets, several sites need to follow one set of asset standards, or the records have to[sync with the ERP](https://upkeep.com/blog/cmms-erp-integration/) , an EAM is the stronger choice.


**Decision dimension**


**CMMS fit**


**EAM fit**


Primary operating job


Execute and control maintenance work


Connect maintenance work to replacement planning, budgets, and other company systems


Asset data scope


Maintenance history and work details


One asset list shared across sites and teams, used for replacement and budget planning


Governance


Local or maintenance-led standards may be sufficient


Cross-site standards, permissions, ownership, and common data rules matter more


System relationships


Limited or focused integrations


ERP, finance, procurement, reliability, data platforms, or other systems are part of the operating model


Implementation burden


Can be narrower when scope and data are simpler


Usually grows with data migration, integrations, rules for who maintains the data, and coordination across teams


An EAM is also a good fit when operations depend heavily on equipment, assets stay in service for many years, you have inspection or compliance obligations, or a reliability program depends on years of consistent history and condition readings.


## **Core Maintenance Capabilities**


Most current platforms share the same maintenance core: asset records and history, work management, preventive maintenance, inspections, parts and inventory, mobile execution, labor tracking, and reporting. These let a team see all open work and follow each procedure the same way to ensure uniformity.


Advanced capabilities vary by software. Condition monitoring, predictive models, capital or project accounting, GIS (e.g., mapping assets spread across a geographic area, such as pipelines or utility poles), EHS (environment, health, and safety) functions, and advanced scheduling matter in certain environments. Which ones you need depends on your industry and the inspections your equipment has to pass:


-


**Hospitals:** EHS incident reporting, plus the generator and medical gas inspection records that accreditation surveys check


-


**Food and Beverage Plants:** Condition monitoring on refrigeration, plus the instrument calibration records that food safety audits check


-


**Airports:** GIS for runway lights, taxiway signs, and other airfield assets, with inspection histories for regulators


-


**Utilities:** Capital project accounting for long replacement programs, and GIS for pipelines and poles


-


**Manufacturing Plants:** Predictive models fed by vibration and temperature readings from critical production lines


### **Out-of-the-Box or Custom EAM?**


An out-of-the-box EAM still needs configuration. Without writing code, your team sets up its own fields, forms, work order types, approval steps, and reports, while standard maintenance work requires nothing more. Custom code makes sense when a core process can’t be built through configuration, such as a regulated inspection scored with your engineers’ own formulas. It costs more to build and test, and every upgrade has to carry it forward. Before paying for a custom option, ask each vendor to show how much of that process they can build with configuration alone.


## **How to Evaluate EAM Maintenance Software**


When considering EAM maintenance software, bring one real job to every demo, such as a recurring pump failure, and ask the vendor to walk through it in entirety. It should cover the request or alarm and the threshold that triggers it, planning (i.e., scheduling the job, assigning a technician, and reserving parts), the technician’s work, closeout, the asset history it leaves behind, and any handoff to finance or purchasing. Work through these criteria before and during the demos:


-


**Operating Scope:** Define the jobs the platform must handle immediately, like daily work orders and scheduled inspections for one plant, and what it must support next, such as replacement planning across three sites.


-


**Advanced Capabilities:** Ask whether each advanced feature your industry needs is included, on a higher plan, or sold separately.


-


**Compliance Support:** Have the vendor pull one asset’s inspection history the way an auditor would, including who signed off and when, what they found, and how a defect was fixed.


-


**Asset-Data Model:** Check if the system can accommodate how your organization organizes assets, including locations, parent-child relationships (e.g., a motor recorded under the conveyor it drives),[criticality ratings](https://upkeep.com/blog/criticality-maintenance-strategy/) (how much a failure would disrupt operations or drive up costs), naming conventions, custom attributes, and history.


-


**Integrations:** Ask how the system connects to your ERP, procurement, finance, sensor, and login (single sign-on) systems, and which of those integrations come built in and which need custom work. Agree up front which system’s record counts for each kind of data, usually the ERP for part costs and the EAM for work history, and correct the other system to match.


-


**Field Use:** Have the lead technician try mobile work orders, offline mode, QR scans, photos, and checklists where work happens, such as a basement mechanical room with no signal. When closing a job on a phone is quick, technicians do it on the spot while the details are fresh.


-


**Permissions and Approvals:** Review who can change records at each site and which actions need approval, and confirm a planner at any site can add a new asset right away and have it reviewed afterward.


-


**Total Cost:** Add data cleanup, migration, integrations, setup, training, and administration to the subscription price, plus hosting and IT time if the system runs on your own servers.


-


**Data Export:** Have the vendor export a few of your assets with their work orders and history the way you’d need them if you switched systems.


## **The True Extent of “Free” EAM Software**


A “free” EAM usually means one of five arrangements, and each one leaves different work for your team. Before comparing one with a paid platform, check what the free offer includes and which costs move to you, such as hosting, administration, integrations, support, and upgrades.


**Free model**


**What it usually means**


**What to evaluate**

Which actions require paid seats and whether the free roles cover what your team needs to do

## **AI, Condition Monitoring, and Predictive Maintenance**


Predictive tools in EAM software are easiest to judge on a single machine. Take[a vibration sensor](https://upkeep.com/blog/vibration-analysis-for-predictive-maintenance/) on a mixer gearbox: If it registers a reading above its set limit, the system raises an alert either directly or through a predictive model. A planner then opens a work order. Every step depends on accurate asset records, alert limits set from each machine’s normal readings, someone confirming each alert is real, and a named person who acts on it. With all four elements in place, technicians spend their time working on equipment whose readings show a genuine problem.


The most reliable savings estimate for your site comes from your own equipment, since[published condition monitoring evaluations](https://www.nist.gov/publications/comprehensive-evaluations-condition-monitoring-based-technologies-industrial) measure savings and performance in different ways. Pick one critical asset, take its last unplanned failure, and add up the downtime and repair cost an early warning would have avoided.


## **How to Tell the Rollout Is Working**


The first sign a new EAM system is working is that people trust and use it, while reliability numbers like mean time between failures take longer to move. Track the five measures below from the trial import of your data through the first weeks after go-live, when the new system fully takes over.


**Measure**


**What it shows**


**How to track it**


Records matched at go-live


Whether every asset and open job came across complete


Share of records that match between the old and new systems after the trial import and again at go-live


PM schedules active at go-live


Whether planned work continues without a gap


Share of migrated PM tasks with an asset, a frequency, and a next due date


Work orders closed on mobile


Whether technicians record work as it happens


Share of work orders closed from a phone or tablet by the technician who did the job


Requests entered in the system


Whether requesters have moved off phone calls and email


Share of new maintenance requests submitted through the system each week


Training completed by role


Whether every user practiced their daily tasks before go-live


Share of technicians, planners, and requesters trained before go-live


## **How to Migrate Your Data and Train Your Team**


Your implementation plan sets the goals and determines if you win each team’s buy-in. Follow the seven steps below to get every asset cleaned and matched to its new identifier and every role trained before go-live:


1.


**Prepare the Asset List:** Before any data moves, the rollout lead (often the maintenance manager) and an asset administrator, who keeps the asset list current after go-live, agree on the[asset hierarchy](https://upkeep.com/learning/asset-hierarchy/) and one naming rule for asset identifiers. They also name an owner for each type of data, like the reliability engineer for criticality ratings.


2.


**Decide What to Move:** The rollout lead and a planner choose the records, such as assets, open work orders, PM schedules, parts, vendors, and the history your next replacement decisions will need. Retire outdated PM tasks before the import, or they’ll carry across with everything else. This is also the time to adopt[run-to-failure maintenance](https://upkeep.com/blog/what-is-run-to-failure-maintenance/) for any low-criticality assets that cost less to replace than to keep servicing.


3.


**Clean the Data and Match Identifiers:** The asset administrator removes duplicates, fills in missing locations, gets missing criticality ratings from the reliability engineer, and builds a list showing the new identifier that replaces each old one. “Line 3 Labeler” in the old spreadsheet becomes “LBL-03” and keeps its full repair history. With an UpKeep[implementation package](https://upkeep.com/pricing/) , you can hand the identifier list, the cleanup, and the migration to UpKeep’s team so you don’t have to worry about it.


4.


**Run a Trial Import, Then Compare Totals:** Before go-live, the vendor or IT runs a trial import, and the asset administrator compares counts of assets, open jobs, and parts with the old system and spot-checks PM due dates. Each difference is a record to fix while the old system still runs. For instance, after Amtrak’s inspector general compared two of the railroad’s asset systems, the company raised the share of substations listed in both from 47% to 96% by correcting its records.


5.


**Train Each Role on Its Daily Tasks:** In the weeks before go-live, the rollout lead runs short sessions by role on equipment people already know. Technicians close a work order on a phone with parts, labor, and the failure cause, planners build next week’s schedule, and requesters submit a test request. After go-live, a[superuser](https://upkeep.com/blog/cmms-superuser-training/) on each shift, usually a planner or supervisor, answers questions.


6.


**Switch Systems at Go-Live:** On the day, the rollout lead closes the old system to new entries, and the vendor or IT moves the last open work orders across. The old system stays read-only for a few months so planners can look up older history.


7.


**Review Progress After Go-Live:** Every two weeks, the asset administrator checks[data quality](https://upkeep.com/blog/cmms-data-quality/) , such as duplicate assets and work orders closed without parts or labor, along with the rollout measures above. Once two checks in a row turn up no new duplicates or incomplete closeouts, the review cadence can move to quarterly.


## **From Repeat Repairs to Planned Replacements**


When each site keeps its own records, a cooling tower fan can go through three rebuilds before anyone totals what it’s cost the company, and leaders can’t compare equipment because they have different names across sites.


With one shared asset record in an EAM system, planners can see how often the fan has failed between rebuilds before they schedule the next one. Finance weighs a replacement request against every rebuild on the fan’s record. The rising repair spend reaches the budget meeting ahead of the next breakdown, and the replacement goes into a planned shutdown.


With UpKeep, the fan’s earlier rebuilds come across in the migration, and from go-live on, technicians log each new repair from a phone at the cooling tower.

## **FAQ**


### **Is EAM maintenance software the same as a CMMS?**


No, though they overlap. Both keep asset history, run work orders, and schedule preventive maintenance, and many CMMS platforms now handle several sites and mobile work. EAM software fits better when finance, purchasing, and several sites all rely on the same maintenance records, such as using repair costs to budget replacements. Start from which teams need your records.


### **Does a multi-site maintenance team automatically need EAM?**


No. Running multiple sites is one signal, and it points toward EAM when those sites need shared asset standards, common rules for who can change data, integrations with company-wide systems, or each asset’s history from purchase to retirement. Sites that run independently and only need reliable day-to-day maintenance tracking can do well with a CMMS.


### **Can free EAM software be used in production?**


Yes. Certain $0 plans, open-source packages, and free self-hosted editions can run day-to-day maintenance work. Whether one fits depends on its user and asset limits, its integrations, the support available, and whether your team can handle hosting, security updates, and administration long term. Check those limits against your full crew and asset count before your team starts logging real work.


### **Is predictive maintenance a standard EAM feature?**


No. Many EAM and CMMS products offer condition monitoring and predictive features, often as add-ons or on higher plans, and others connect to a separate sensor platform. Before paying for one, ask what data it needs, who on your team checks its predictions, and how its alerts become work orders in your system.


### **How much work history should we migrate?**


Bring over every open work order and active preventive maintenance schedule so no planned job drops at go-live. For closed work, bring enough history to support the first big decision on the calendar, such as next quarter’s replacement request for a critical asset. Older records can stay in the old system while it’s read-only, and planners can search them there.
